catalog_quote: Stress is phonemic, as is shown by the following contrasts: /'sikaal/ it is a long way /si'kaal/ fish type; /'miyil/ to a tree /mi'yil/ banana tree; /'asadiy/ they are dogs /asadi'yaay/ nettle bush. Although stress is not predictable it has a strong grammatical patterning in that its most frequent occurrence is on the final syllable of stems. Each example following contains one stem with its affixes set off by hyphens: /a-'waal/ (imperative prefix — to go up) go up! /'kaagʷ-ad/ (small drum — it is) it is a small drum /ya'ga-na/ (to be afraid — she) she is afraid /tapʷi'ya-na-ñin/ (to shave head — present — you) you are shaving a head. Certain one-syllable verb stems form an exception to this pattern. When these are affixed with the present tense morpheme /-na/, which in turn is always followed by a person morpheme, the stress falls on the /-na/ as follows: /gʷa/ to dig out grass /gʷa-'n…

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is contrastive/lexical (minimal pairs), with a strong tendency to fall on the final syllable of the stem (affixes normally unstressed); the stressed syllable carries the pitch peak. Corroborated by the modern reference grammar, Aikhenvald 2008 ch.1 sec.1.1 (saved): 'Stress is movable and contrastive. Long vowels tend to be stressed (Chapter 2).'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed by Allen & Hurd; Aikhenvald ch.1 silent (details in her ch.2, not accessible).
new_statements.exceptions: Certain monosyllabic verb stems: with present-tense -na (always followed by a person suffix) stress falls on -na (gʷa-'na-ñin 'you are digging grass', la-'na-diy 'they are cutting'). Aikhenvald adds that long vowels tend to attract stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (stem plus affixes, examples given as affixed words in isolation); intonation treated separately in sec.3.2.
new_statements.identity_note: Allen & Hurd's data are from Yambon (Yuanab) village, 1962-63, one of the five Manambu villages (Avatip, Yawabak, Malu, Apa:n, Yambon); Laycock 1965 and Allen & Hurd report no dialect differences. Aikhenvald 2008 is based mainly on Avatip. All refer to Manambu proper, glottocode mana1298 / ISO mle.

sources.note: p.41 sec.3.1: stress is phonemic (minimal pairs 'sikaal vs si'kaal etc.); not predictable but most frequently on the final syllable of stems; exception: certain monosyllabic verb stems shift stress to present-tense -na; pitch peak on the stressed syllable. Fieldwork 1962-63, Yambon village.

sources.note: No Manambu stress-placement rule; says phonetic values are 'similar to those of Wosera, except as noted below' and mentions stress-conditioned allophony of /r/ and of /wA/ ('pronounced as a single phone in stressed positions'). Wosera (Abelam) non-phonemic stress rule is in sec.5.2 pp.29-30, not asserted for Manambu.
